related_questions.question: What tests are done to check for uterine cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: To diagnose uterine cancer, doctors primarily use endometrial tissue sampling (biopsy) and imaging tests like ultrasound. Other tests, such as hysteroscopy, dilation and curettage (D&C), and various imaging scans, may also be employed.
snippet_highlighted_words: endometrial tissue sampling (biopsy) and imaging tests like ultrasound

list.title: Endometrial Biopsy:
list.snippet: This is the most common test for diagnosing endometrial cancer. A small sample of the uterine lining (endometrium) is removed and examined under a microscope for cancer cells.

list.title: Hysteroscopy:
list.snippet: A thin, telescope-like instrument (hysteroscope) is inserted into the uterus to visualize the uterine lining. A biopsy can be taken during this procedure.

list.title: Dilation and Curettage (D&C):
list.snippet: If a biopsy doesn't provide enough tissue or the results are unclear, a D&C may be performed. This involves dilating the cervix and using a curette to scrape tissue from the uterine lining.
Pelvic Ultrasound: Uses sound waves to create images of the uterus and surrounding organs.
Transvaginal Ultrasound: A specialized ultrasound where the probe is inserted into the vagina to get a closer look at the uterus.
CT Scan: Creates detailed cross-sectional images of the body using X-rays.
MRI: Uses magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of organs and tissues.
PET Scan: Can help detect cancer spread by showing areas of increased metabolic activity.
Chest X-ray: May be used to check for cancer spread to the lungs.

list.title: Cystoscopy and Proctoscopy:
list.snippet: May be used if uterine cancer is suspected to have spread to the bladder or rectum.

list.title: Blood tests:
list.snippet: May be used to check for tumor markers like CA-125, which can be elevated in some cases of uterine cancer.
After a diagnosis, further tests are often needed to determine the stage and grade of the cancer. This helps determine the best treatment options.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that there are no routine screening tests for uterine cancer like there are for cervical cancer (Pap smears). If you have symptoms or risk factors, it's crucial to discuss them with your doctor to determine the appropriate tests for diagnosis and management.

related_questions.title: Endometrial (Uterine) Cancer Screening Guidelines

text_blocks.snippet: Uterine cancer screening typically involves tests like endometrial biopsy or transvaginal ultrasound, particularly for women experiencing symptoms or those at high risk. Screening is not routinely recommended for all women due to the potential for false positives and the lack of proven benefit in the general population.
snippet_highlighted_words: typically involves tests like endometrial biopsy or transvaginal ultrasound

list.title: High-risk individuals:
list.snippet: Women with a family history of Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) or other risk factors (like obesity, a high-fat diet, or certain reproductive factors) are often recommended for screening.

list.title: Symptomatic women:
list.snippet: If a woman experiences unusual vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, or other symptoms that could indicate uterine cancer, she should consult her doctor for evaluation.

list.title: Older women:
list.snippet: Uterine cancer is more common in older women, particularly those who have gone through menopause.

list.title: Endometrial Biopsy:
list.snippet: This procedure involves taking a small sample of the uterine lining for microscopic examination. It is often done in a doctor's office.

list.title: Transvaginal Ultrasound:
list.snippet: This imaging test uses sound waves to create pictures of the uterus, and can help detect abnormalities.

list.title: Other tests:
list.snippet: In some cases, other tests like hysteroscopy, dilation and curettage (D&C), or imaging scans (like chest x-rays or barium enemas) may be used to further investigate the extent of the cancer if it is suspected.

list.title: False results:
list.snippet: Screening tests can sometimes produce false-negative (cancer is present but not detected) or false-positive (cancer is not present but test suggests it is) results.

list.title: Potential risks:
list.snippet: Some screening tests can cause discomfort or other side effects.

list.title: Individualized approach:
list.snippet: The decision to screen should be made in consultation with a healthcare provider, taking into account individual risk factors and potential benefits and risks.

list.title: Research on new tests:
list.snippet: Research is ongoing to develop new, less invasive screening methods, such as the tampon-based test being explored by Mayo Clinic researchers.
